chapter_theme: The search for Udayana's vanished divine elephant is set beside Pradyota's court in Ujjain, where, enraged by a tribute-roll and by his ministers' praise of Udayana, the king lets them build a mechanical elephant packed with ninety-six armed men; Udayana ignores omens and Vayantakan's warning, plays his veena before it, and is surrounded.

cast.role: Udayana, the Vatsa king who is hunting for his lost divine elephant (called வத்தவன், உதையன்)
the Vatsa king's minister who rules while he is absorbed in plays (verse 29, uncertain)
Udayana's companion who warns him and brings five hundred heroes
King of Ujjain who rules with the discus and plots against Udayana
Pradyota's ministers, who praise Udayana and then build the decoy
Pradyota's minister who rides the artificial elephant and is sent with it
the ninety-six armed men hidden inside the machine elephant
the hunters and forest-dwellers who see the decoy and report it
Udayana's army that searches for the lost elephant

29.reading: The king's minister, dear to him, drives out the swarming enemies and runs the realm in the king's name, while the king, watching rare plays and sunk in feeling, forgets Karinam and dines with his beloved.
29.nuance: The verse sets the minister's labour beside the king's ease in one sentence, so the loss in the next verse follows a stretch of heedless pleasure. The word அமைச்சியன் is not a name; that it is Yugi, as verse 38 suggests, is an inference.
29.event: While his minister crushes the enemies and rules for him, the king, absorbed in plays, forgets Karinam and eats a meal with his beloved.

30.reading: The lasting divine elephant vanishes by magic; the king, spent like a serpent that has lost its jewel, falls into grief, bids the elephant be sought, and the great army goes searching all over the earth.
30.event: The divine elephant disappears and Udayana orders his army to search the whole land for it.

31.reading: Where the waters of the Sindhu and the Ganga join and feed the land, in the fair country of Avanti, stands the rich fortified city Ujjain, whose crowding mansions touch the moon.
31.nuance: The scene moves to Ujjain; the story of Udayana's side stops while the rival's court is set out.

32.reading: Pradyota, whose armies cannot be counted, rules the earth with the discus he bears, while kings in rows bring tribute in wealth, and he stays on with his roaring great elephant and chariot.

33.reading: When the matchless king calls for the gold tribute, he has not seen that a mark has been put against one name on the roll of the kings' tribute; when it is told him he flares up.
33.nuance: The words ஒருமகன் புள்ளி are hard: it may be a single man or a son who made the mark, or a dot against a name. The sense of a mark on the roll is the likely one, but it is not fixed by the line.
33.event: Pradyota calls for tribute, is told of a mark on the tribute-roll that he had missed, and grows angry.

34.reading: His eyes blazing like a lotus on fire, the lord asks his ministers what excuse they have for hiding so well, until he forgot it, the wrong done by the king of the sea-girt land.
34.nuance: The accused is left unnamed in the verse; that the sea-girt king is Udayana comes from the next verses, which praise his gifts. A king who accuses his counsellors of concealing a fact is the case Kural 638 and 639 reverse.
34.event: Pradyota questions his ministers for concealing the offender's act from him.

35.reading: The ministers begin to list what the man has: courage proved in the field, learning that brings gain, his way of checking the fierce-eyed elephant, and his flawless mastery of the veena.
35.nuance: The two skills at the centre of the list, handling elephants and playing the veena, are the ones the ambush later uses against him.
35.event: The ministers name Udayana's skills of arms, learning, elephant-taming and the veena to the angry king.

36.reading: They go on to his inherited wealth, his youth and beauty, his jewels and good family, and say, in measured words, that since he is all this what he did is his due.
36.nuance: The ministers answer the king's accusation by praising the man, not by denying the fault. The sense of உற்ற கடனென, that what he did is fitting to his rank, is doubtful.
36.event: The ministers finish listing Udayana's merits and speak of what is due to him.

37.reading: The king hears and rages, orders them to seize the man who has come and bring him, and the ministers gathered there ask what must be done, then settle among themselves on something else.
37.nuance: The king's anger overrides the ministers' praise at once, and the ministers do not oppose it openly but turn to a scheme.
37.event: Pradyota orders Udayana seized; his ministers instead decide on another plan.

38.reading: The proud ministers take counsel on several matters, Yugi's going to war against the weak foes, the king's pity at the elephant's going, and catching a forest elephant by showing one, and join in one counsel.
38.nuance: The verse names three things on the table; which one they choose has to be read from what they build in the next verses.
38.event: Pradyota's ministers deliberate and agree on a plan of taking an elephant by displaying another.

39.reading: With lac, thread hardened with wax, wood, painted lime and hair, with stretched hide and whatever else they needed, they made an elephant with their own hands.
39.nuance: The materials are the ones used for dolls and models: the elephant is made to be taken for a real one, not for use as a siege engine.
39.event: The ministers build an artificial elephant out of lac, thread, wood, hair and hide.

40.reading: A mechanical elephant with levers and a swollen belly holds ninety-six men, weapons hidden, and they drive it along the road like a blue mountain.
40.nuance: The men inside are the weapon and the elephant a shell: its likeness to a real elephant is its only force.
40.event: Ninety-six armed men hide inside the mechanical elephant and drive it on.

41.reading: As the elephant trumpets like thunder, the minister Salankayan, one of the ministers, rides the battle-elephant before the king and shows it.
41.event: Salankayan rides the artificial elephant before Pradyota to show it to him.

42.reading: At the ruler's word, Salankayan, go and bring it, he sets off swiftly with spear, with the white umbrella, the sceptre and the feather fan of kings.
42.nuance: That Salankayan carries the king's insignia may mark him as the king's envoy or may be a part of the disguise; the verse does not say.
42.event: Pradyota sends Salankayan out; he sets off carrying royal insignia.

43.reading: Sixteen thousand elephants of the eight hills, sixteen thousand fine horses, sixteen thousand decorated chariots and sixteen thousand archers go with them.
43.nuance: The word எண்வரை before elephants is rare and its sense (of eight kinds, or of the eight hills) is not fixed here.
43.event: A force of sixteen thousand each of elephants, horses, chariots and archers is named to go with the machine.

44.reading: With all this in good order, the one who sends them says come softly, and the elephant of well-made levers arrives in the forest of the Vatsa king.
44.nuance: The verse does not name who gives the order to come softly; it may be the king or Salankayan.
44.event: The artificial elephant and its host are sent to the forest of the Vatsa king.

45.reading: In that forest the hunters look with love at the cow-elephants and at the great bull whose rut sets bees rising, holding a leafy bough in its trunk like a storm cloud.
45.nuance: The decoy is made to behave like a bull in rut, so the shell is dressed in the signs of a living elephant.
45.event: The forest-dwellers see the decoy among the real cow-elephants and take it for a rutting bull.

46.reading: Thinking it is our lord's elephant, they run to tell Udayana; with a splendid horse in jewelled trappings, the proud king mounts and sets out.
46.nuance: Whether எம் இறை means Udayana, as the story of the lost divine elephant would suggest, or only the hunters' lord in general is not fixed in the line.
46.event: The hunters report the elephant to Udayana, thinking it his own, and he rides out.

47.reading: Though birds cross his path and ill signs show, the generous king walks on, Vayantakan holds him back in vain, and in the honey-dripping grove he sees the false elephant and grows glad by words he trusts.
47.nuance: Omens and a warning both reach him before he sees the decoy; the verse offers no excuse for him. The sense of line 4 is not clear.
47.event: Udayana ignores the omens and Vayantakan's warning and walks to the grove where he sees the false elephant.

claims.claim: birds crossing the path and ill signs are warnings of coming harm

48.reading: Without a glance of desire at the company named in line 1, he is glad at heart and plays his great veena, strings true, in the right raga.
48.nuance: He answers a decoy of his own sort with his own art: the skill that the ministers praised is his lure.
48.event: Udayana takes up his veena and plays it in the proper raga.

49.reading: As the music reaches the wide ears of the mechanical elephant and he rides on eagerly, the hidden men burst the hand-made beast, the fittings fall away, and it becomes a fighting host.
49.nuance: The words of line 3 can also be read as the hidden men destroying the elephant's shell for the sake of the attack; the sense is the same.
49.event: The hidden men break out of the machine as Udayana rides in, and it turns into an army.

50.reading: Seeing in the enemy's deed a clever picture, he smiles, and Vayantakan and five hundred faultless heroes come and join him.
50.event: Udayana smiles at the trick and is joined by Vayantakan and five hundred warriors.

51.reading: The army hidden in the elephant spreads out and closes round them; the angry Vatsa king cuts down hundreds, then his own force breaks and dies at the front.
51.nuance: Whose army is meant by சேனை in line 4 is not marked; it may be his own five hundred.
51.event: The hidden host encircles Udayana's party; he kills hundreds before the force at the front is broken.

links.note: Udayana orders the land searched for his vanished divine elephant; the hunters, seeing the decoy, think it is our lord's elephant and run to him.
links.teaches: The search for the lost elephant is what makes the decoy believable, since his own people hurry to bring him the news.

links.note: The ministers settle on taking an elephant by showing one; Udayana walks into the grove and sees the false elephant.
links.teaches: The ministers' choice of lure in 38 is fitted to a king who is hunting for his elephant, which verse 47 shows working.

links.note: The ministers name his elephant-taming and his veena as his glory; in 48 he plays the veena at the decoy.
links.teaches: The skill that makes a man formidable is also his weak point, since his veena is what carries him to the trap.

links.note: The ministers list Udayana's merits to temper the king; the king answers by raging and ordering him seized.
links.teaches: Telling an angry king a rival's merits does not calm him, it sends the ministers toward a plot.

links.note: Ninety-six armed men are put inside the machine in 40; in 49 they break out as it becomes a fighting host.
links.teaches: The machine of 40 is shown to be a hiding place for troops, and 49 is the moment it is turned into one.

links.note: The Kural's picture is of binding a rutting elephant by means of an elephant; verse 40 builds an elephant of wood and hide, filled with ninety-six men, to take a king.
links.teaches: The ministers use the Kural's own method in a worse form, a false elephant with men inside and a king as the catch.

gains.a: a rule for the ruse: using one thing of its own kind to take another, here a false elephant to catch a king who tames real ones
gains.b: a case where the stand-in is a built shell with armed men inside and the quarry is a ruler, not a beast

links.note: The Kural ranks the slackness of great joy below anger as a cause of ruin; in 47 the king goes on though omens and Vayantakan warn him.
links.teaches: The Kural's slackness is not ignorance: Udayana is told and warned, and in the verse it is his gladness at sight of the elephant that wins.

gains.a: a case where the heedless one has both omens and a friend's warning, so slackness is a choice made in delight, not a lapse of knowledge
gains.b: a story in which joy's slackness is shown over a few verses, before the trap closes on a king and a friend who knew better

links.note: The Kural makes it the duty of a minister at the king's side to tell him what is good for him; in 36 the ministers tell Pradyota of Udayana's merits.
links.teaches: The ministers do speak, as the Kural asks, but to a king in anger the truth ends in a plot, so the duty to speak does not guarantee it is heard.

gains.a: a case in which ministers do speak in the king's presence and yet are turned aside
gains.b: a test of the duty to speak when the king, angry, has no wish to be told good of his enemy

links.note: The Kural says a king who does not think matters through with his circle and then lashes out in anger sees his fortune shrink; in 37 Pradyota rages after the ministers have spoken.
links.teaches: The king here has taken counsel and yet his anger still rules the outcome, so the Kural's warning is about whether counsel is heard, not just whether it is asked.

gains.a: a king who does hear his circle and still gives way to rage, which the Kural's rule does not cover
gains.b: a scene in which the king's anger leads at once to a plot rather than to a loss of fortune, as the couplet only warns

source_issues: The order of verses 29 and 30, which belong to Udayana's own court, before verse 31 introduces Ujjain, is not marked by any change of scene in the text.
Verse 48 line 1 has an unclear phrase (நக்க கணத்தை) that is read here as a group he did not look at, which is doubtful.
The word division of the edition splits many words across lines of the verse, as in வனச்சரர் and சாலங்காய.
